_: The feature cards: one entry per feature, and one per part of a feature. main.js shows an entry in the object card when its object is clicked or it's chosen from the panel's Features list; Explore features marks the objects; scripts/14_check_features.mjs checks every entry has its fields, links to an object and names a demo or action that exists. Objects: addon:<id> (an add-on built in addons.js), part:<name> (a part of the room models), placed:<type> (an item from Place items), node:<name> (a named object, such as a wardrobe compartment, which counts only while its door is open), lights (the ceiling lights of the scheme in use), switch (the smart-glass wall switch). After a |, a condition on the room's choices: the object counts for this entry only then. The first object is where Explore's marker goes. A feature worked from a control above the room, with no object of its own, names that control's id in `control` instead. Evidence is either 'Expected, not shown.' or a line with its strength and sources from options.json (sourcesFrom: a group, or group:option). Nothing here is measured: every reading and status on a card is simulated.

features.name: Adaptive circadian lighting
features.purpose: Room light that follows the day: cool and bright by day, warm and dim in the evening.
features.how: Choose Circadian under Lighting. Its white light is tunable. The colour follows the room's solar time: warm at dawn, coolest from 10 am to 3 pm, warm again by 7 pm. From 6:30 pm to 9:30 pm it dims to well under half. The reading light and the examination task light keep their own switches.
features.benefit: A clearer day and night, and less bright light when the patient should be asleep.
features.awake: It follows the day, and the reading light is still there for a book.
features.sedated: It follows the day all the same. Staff set the light for care.
features.limits: Light alone isn't shown to prevent delirium. Care comes first: Clinical and Emergency-ready modes switch to full, neutral light.

evidence.text: Mixed. A pilot in redesigned rooms with dynamic light saw less delirium, but the rooms changed in other ways too. A randomised trial of bright dynamic light alone found no effect.
evidence.strength: Observational pilot; randomised trial, stopped early for futility

features.name: Privacy system
features.purpose: Privacy at the glazed front and the window when the patient needs it. Staff can end it at once.
features.how: With smart glass on the glazed front, the wall switch or Privacy mode turns the glass opaque, so no fabric curtain is needed. Privacy mode also lowers the window blinds halfway. A curtain or blinds front is closed by hand. Emergency-ready clears the glass.
features.benefit: Dignity during care, washing and rest, without a curtain to launder.
features.awake: The patient can ask for privacy, and for it to end.
features.sedated: Staff use it during care, and clear the glass to look in.
features.limits: Opaque glass hides the patient from the corridor, so staff decide when it's used. In an isolation room the door still needs its seal and pressure tests.

evidence.text: Memorial Sloan Kettering's ICU replaced curtains with switchable glass and reported easier cleaning and better infection control.

features.name: Patient orientation display
features.purpose: The TV can show the weekday, the date, the time of day and whether it's day or night, with a few calm lines beside them: where the patient is, visiting confirmed by staff, and what's planned. Large enough to read from the bed.
features.how: Choose Orientation under Entertainment. The time comes from the room's own sun, and the screen is darker at night. Beside it: a line about where the patient is, visiting information marked as confirmed by staff, a non-urgent plan, and a recovery note when the patient is recovering. Family can add a line, if staff confirm it. It never shows a name, a diagnosis or care information.
features.benefit: Knowing the day and the time without having to ask.
features.awake: Readable from the pillow. Patient view shows what the patient sees.
features.sedated: It stays calm, and darker at night, with nothing that asks for attention.
features.limits: It makes no claim about delirium or sleep. The lines are samples: a real screen would show only what staff have confirmed, and never patient details.

features.name: Nature and environmental display
features.purpose: Calm, natural things to look at from the bed: a scene on the TV, a sky on the ceiling, a digital aquarium and a printed leaf panel.
features.how: Each is its own choice. The TV's scene and the aquarium are original animations drawn in the page. The sky is a lit panel above the bed. The leaf panel is placed from Place items. None brings soil, water or animals into the room.
features.benefit: Something restful to look at, instead of equipment and a blank ceiling.
features.awake: The patient can choose what's on, or turn it off.
features.sedated: Staff choose, and keep it still and quiet.
features.limits: Emergency-ready turns the screens off. Living plants and fish tanks stay out of patient-care areas, as CDC guidance advises.

features.name: TV nature scene
features.purpose: An original animation on the TV: desert dunes under a slowly moving sun.
features.how: Choose On under Entertainment, TV. It's drawn in the page at a slow frame rate, and only while the TV is in view.
features.benefit: A slow, natural scene to rest the eyes on.
features.limits: Placeholder content, not real footage. Emergency-ready turns it off.

features.name: Sky ceiling
features.purpose: A printed sky on the ceiling above the bed, lit from behind.
features.how: Choose Printed sky under Ceiling above the bed. The panel is 3 by 2.2 m, centred over the bed, and it glows without the room lights.
features.benefit: Something to look up at that isn't a light fitting or a ceiling grid.
features.limits: A real panel needs a wipe-clean face and a fixing the ceiling can take.

features.name: Digital aquarium
features.purpose: Animated fish on a wall screen, with no water, fish or servicing in the room.
features.how: Choose Digital screen under Aquarium. The fish are drawn in the page, and move only while the screen is in view.
features.benefit: The calm of watching fish, with nothing to clean or keep alive.
features.limits: CDC guidance says to avoid fish tanks in patient-care areas, which is why it's a screen. Emergency-ready turns it off.

features.name: Biophilic wall panel
features.purpose: Greenery without soil or water: a printed leaf scene behind a sealed, wipe-clean acrylic face. Living plants stay outside the glass.
features.how: Place it from Place items, on any clear stretch of wall. It's about 0.9 by 1.2 m, centred 1.7 m up, clear of wall ledges.
features.benefit: Green to look at, from something that's cleaned like any other surface.
features.limits: CDC guidance says not to allow fresh flowers or potted plants in patient-care areas for immunosuppressed patients, so real plants stay outside.

features.name: Built-in sliding wardrobe
features.purpose: Compact, organised storage for the patient's clothing, belongings and daily necessities, built in floor to ceiling against the back wall, clear of the entry route.
features.how: Two flush sliding doors on two tracks, so one side opens at a time: the left door runs behind the right. Behind them, a compartment for each use: daily essentials on a shelf at eye level, a lockable box for valuables, room for a bag, and a rail for clothes. A low-glare light comes on inside when a door opens. Flush end and filler panels make it read as joinery, and a fixed panel over the doors hides the track and leaves no top for dust. A real one would need the wall, services, infection-control requirements and emergency clearances checked.
features.benefit: Belongings kept organised, private and easy to find, and out of sight, so the room looks less cluttered.
features.awake: The patient knows where their things are, and can ask for them.
features.sedated: Nurses or authorised caregivers reach belongings for the patient.
features.limits: It takes about the same floor area as the freestanding wardrobe it replaced: what it adds is height, easier cleaning and a tidier look. A design concept: no inventory display or electronic lock is modelled.

features.name: Clothing
features.purpose: A dedicated area for clean patient clothing and personal garments, keeping belongings organised and separate from clinical supplies.
features.how: A hanging rail behind the right-hand door, with room for shoes below it.
features.benefit: Clothes kept clean, together and ready to wear.
features.limits: Patient clothing only: clinical supplies are kept elsewhere.

features.name: Daily essentials
features.purpose: An accessible shelf for items such as glasses, books and approved everyday necessities.
features.how: A shelf at eye level behind the left-hand door, about 1.5 m up, within reach of someone standing.
features.benefit: Less searching for the things used every day.
features.limits: What may be kept at the bedside is the ward's decision.

features.name: Personal belongings
features.purpose: A section for bags and other permitted belongings, keeping the room organised.
features.how: Space on the cabinet floor behind the left-hand door, for a bag or a small case.
features.benefit: A bag has its own place, instead of standing on the floor.
features.limits: Only permitted belongings: the ward decides what can stay.

features.name: Secure valuables
features.purpose: A separately controlled box for permitted valuables.
features.how: A lockable box on a low shelf behind the left-hand door. In this model the keypad is drawn on, and nothing locks.
features.benefit: Valuables kept apart from everyday things, out of sight.
features.limits: In real hospital use, storage and access must follow institutional security policies.

features.name: Cabinet lighting
features.purpose: Low-glare light inside the cabinet, for finding belongings in dim conditions.
features.how: A warm strip under the inside top. In this model it comes on while a door is open.
features.benefit: Staff can find things without turning on the room lights.
features.limits: It can be turned off, so it doesn't disturb the patient's rest. No switch or sensor is modelled.

features.name: Sliding doors
features.purpose: Flush sliding doors, which open without swinging out into the room.
features.how: Two doors on two tracks, hung from above behind the fixed panel, with a guide at the foot. One side opens at a time.
features.benefit: Nothing swings into the space where staff work.
features.limits: The freestanding wardrobe it replaced had sliding doors too, so the mechanism isn't new.

features.name: Patient states
features.purpose: The room follows the patient: sedated or unresponsive, awake, or recovering. A control above the room, beside the room modes.
features.how: Sedated: steady light by the time of day, a little lower, and nothing on the patient's screen; staff set comfort and see the positioning reminder, line status and noise. Awake: the room as configured, with the patient's own controls, communication, privacy and family. Recovering: the orientation screen first, light by the time of day, simple choices. Changes ease over a few seconds. The room modes stay as they are: Clinical and Emergency-ready are the staff override and always win.
features.benefit: What the patient sees and hears suits what they can take in.
features.awake: The patient's own controls and choices.
features.sedated: Steady light and no entertainment. Comfort is set by staff.
features.limits: Staff decide the state: the room never works it out from the patient. It changes no alarm, device or clinical setting, and it changes no choice or link.

features.name: Communication board
features.purpose: Large buttons for a patient who can't speak: I need help, I am in pain, I feel cold, I feel hot, I need repositioning, I want to contact my family, I need a nurse.
features.how: On the bedside tablet, or on any bedside screen. Three ways to choose: touch; a single switch, while a highlight steps through the buttons; or gaze, where a look held on a button chooses it. Here the switch and gaze are simulated. Each request goes to a nurse-side list with the time, and stays there until a nurse acknowledges it.
features.benefit: A patient who can't speak can still ask for what they need.
features.awake: The patient chooses by touch, a switch or gaze.
features.sedated: Not offered: staff watch for signs instead.
features.limits: Simulated. It does not replace a certified nurse-call system: a real one is wired, tested and maintained to its own standard. No request leaves this page.

features.name: Personal comfort passport
features.purpose: A sample record of what a patient would like: light, temperature, music or quiet, a nature scene, family photographs, privacy, how they communicate, and entertainment.
features.how: Recorded with the patient or their family. It keeps the patient's preferences apart from the settings the care team controls, and shows how each preference is used or held back in each patient state. Save it in this browser, or restore the sample. It's its own record: Tune it in and PACS keep theirs.
features.benefit: Staff can see at a glance what the patient likes, even when the patient can't say.
features.sedated: Most are held back; staff use some, if they judge them right.
features.limits: A sample for a made-up patient, with no name. Temperature is shown, not applied: no approved limits were supplied. Saved only in this browser, never sent.

features.name: Family connection
features.purpose: Family close by on the bedside screens: photographs, a video call, a voice message, a personal scene, familiar music and a line on the orientation screen.
features.how: Drawn photographs stand in for real ones. The video call and voice message are simulated: shown, not played, because there's no real voice to use. The personal scene goes on the TV, and familiar music plays as demo sound, only when pressed. Staff have Quiet now, which turns all stimulation off, sound included. For an unresponsive patient it offers only what staff allow.
features.benefit: Familiar faces, voices and music, when the patient can take them in.
features.limits: No photograph is uploaded, no camera or microphone is used, and nothing is sent. A real call would need the hospital's approved system.

features.name: Sound-level sensor
features.purpose: A closed door keeps a patient's voice in. This sensor concept gives that hearing back: it would recognise a groan or a call for help and put a notice in front of the nurse outside, who looks in through the glass before deciding to enter. Simulated here by the two buttons.

W1.purpose: A closed isolation door keeps the air in, and the patient's voice with it. This sensor concept gives that hearing back: it would recognise a groan or a call for help and put a notice in front of the nurse outside, who looks in through the glass before deciding to enter. Simulated here by the two buttons.

features.how: The sensor would classify sounds on the device. A call for help asks for a look now. One groan asks for a look when the nurse can, and a third within a minute for a look now. Its light changes colour, and the notice says what was heard. The nurse decides whether to go in.
features.benefit: A patient behind a closed door can still be heard.
features.awake: A call for help reaches the nurse without a button.
features.sedated: Ventilated or sedated patients may make no sound. Quiet is never a sign that all is well.

features.name: Room comfort control
features.purpose: A wall-mounted temperature and humidity control concept. It is not connected to room equipment or patient measurements. The air behind it is cleaned in the plant room, out of sight:
features.how: The Comfort systems section has two SIMULATED sliders, for temperature and humidity. They change this control's status light: blue when cool, amber when warm. Nothing is heated, cooled or measured.
features.benefit: One place by the door where staff can see the room's comfort settings.
features.limits: No hospital-approved temperature limits were supplied, so nothing is set from here. Cleaning the air is the plant room's job.

features.name: Daylight sensor
features.purpose: A small light sensor on the window sill. It tells Comfort mode and PACS whether daylight is coming in.
features.how: By day, Comfort mode lowers the blinds against glare. After sunset there's no glare to block, so Comfort mode and PACS leave the blinds alone and change only the lighting. In this model the sun's height at the room's solar hour stands in for its reading.
features.benefit: The blinds don't close on an evening view for no reason.
features.limits: A concept: it isn't connected to anything, and it reads nothing here.

features.name: Acoustic comfort mode
features.purpose: A picture of the room's sound: where it comes from, where it's loudest, and what acoustic fittings would change. Simulated.
features.how: Press Acoustic comfort mode above the room. Labels mark six simulated sources: monitor tones, infusion pumps, the ventilator, equipment fans, the door and talk in the corridor, and the two loudest at the pillow are marked. A sound map colours the floor, a ring marks a quiet zone round the bed, and the sound sensor shows a level. Without fittings and With fittings compare the room. The map uses the simplest distance rule: 6 dB quieter each time the distance from a source doubles. Demo sound plays only when asked.
features.benefit: Shows where the room's noise comes from, so a team can see what to change first.
features.awake: A restful sound can play, if staff decide it suits the patient. It never plays over a notice or an alarm.
features.sedated: Nothing here touches the patient's equipment: its alarms and settings stay as they are.
features.limits: Not a measurement: no microphone is used, and nothing listens. Every level is illustrative, and the fittings' effect is made up. Critical alarms are always sounding and visible, and the comfort system has no control over them.

evidence.text: Every ICU in a five-unit study was louder than WHO's hospital guideline, which its authors judged out of reach in an ICU. The fittings' effect is expected, not shown.
evidence.strength: Observational study of five UK ICUs

features.name: Acoustic panels
features.purpose: Wipe-clean panels on the wall and ceiling that absorb some of the sound bouncing round the room.
features.how: Two panels on the family zone's back wall and three ceiling tiles over it, clear of the vents, the lights and the bed. A sealed face over the absorber, wiped like any other surface. Choose them under Acoustic fittings.
features.benefit: Less of every sound bounces back into the room.
features.limits: Their effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off.

features.name: Acoustic partition
features.purpose: The glazed front in laminated acoustic glass, sealed all round: staff still see in, and less corridor talk comes through.
features.how: Laminated glass with a sound-damping layer, and seals round the opening. It stays clear glass, so the smart glass and the curtain still work. Choose it under Acoustic fittings.
features.benefit: Corridor talk stays outside, and the view in stays open.
features.limits: Its effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off. An isolation room's door still needs its own seal and pressure tests.

features.name: Soft-close door and cabinets
features.purpose: Dampers that slow the door and cabinet doors over their last few centimetres, so they don't bang.
features.how: A damper at the head of the room's door, and in the wardrobe's track. The door still closes and seals by itself. Choose it under Acoustic fittings.
features.benefit: No bang when a door shuts at night.
features.limits: Its effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off. It must never stop a door closing fully.

features.name: Vibration-damping mounts
features.purpose: Rubber isolators behind non-critical kit, here the TV, so a hum doesn't carry into the wall.
features.how: Isolators between the TV's bracket and the wall. Never on the monitor, the pumps, the ventilator or any medical device. Choose them under Acoustic fittings.
features.benefit: Less hum carried through the wall.
features.limits: Non-critical kit only. Their effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off.
